english.html: agreed by the said de Rols to be true, and since verified, that the hose were still there.

I do not remember having read that any man had a memory so happy as to remember so many particular acts, places and words, from so long a time, and in regard to so many persons, save the Emperor Hadrian <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. For Cyrus, King of the Persians, being in his great and numerous army, could well tell all the names of his soldiers and men-at-arms, and, reviewing his army, spoke to each one by his name <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Which Lucius Scipio also once did well at Rome <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. Mithridates well remembered twenty-two languages, of as many nations as he had under him, speaking to each one without an interpreter <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. Cineas, ambassador of Pyrrhus, in one day that he was at Rome, learned well all the names of the Roman Senators and knights <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. Seneca could well, as he himself boasts, recite two thousand names in the same order in which they had been pronounced to him, and two hundred verses backwards, beginning from the last <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. Which before him Theodectes, disciple of Aristotle <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>, and Metrodorus the Philosopher (who flourished in the time of Diogenes the Cynic) also did well <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>. One likewise praises much the memory of Julius Caesar, Scipio, Lucullus, Hortensius and Porcius Latro, Romans; and of Themistocles, Carneades and Charmides, Greeks <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. But the memory of this du Tilh here, whether he had gained it by art or by practice, surpassed [theirs], as it seems, he having never been found by the commissioners to have failed by a single iota. Which I mean to have written with the protestation I have made above <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>, of not wishing to enter into comparison of so impudent a cheat with persons so noble, great and illustrious.

notes.citation: Dio Cassius, Roman History, book 69 (69.3, on Hadrian), and Aelius Spartianus, Life of Hadrian in the Historia Augusta (20.7–8)
notes.original: Dion, & Spartiã en la vie d'Adrian.
notes.gloss: Hadrian's memory: he recalled the names of veterans and of many men at once, and Spartianus says he could recite a book after one hearing.

notes.original: Herodote au liure in ſcript. Clio.
notes.gloss: The anecdote of Cyrus knowing every soldier by name is not in Herodotus in Coras's terms; it is Xenophon's (Cyropaedia 5.3.46–47), and is repeated by Pliny (Natural History 7.24.88), Quintilian (11.2.50) and Solinus. The attribution is given as printed.

notes.citation: Solinus, Collectanea rerum memorabilium (the Polyhistor), chapter 7 as cited (the passage on memory is in chapter 1 of the modern division, §§ 106–108; number unverified)
notes.original: Solin en ſon Polhiſt. c. vij.
notes.gloss: Lucius Scipio knew the names of the whole Roman people; the same chapter of Solinus is cited at annot-035 {a}.

notes.original: Appian Ale xandrin. en la Guerre Mithridatique.
notes.gloss: Mithridates spoke the languages of the twenty-two nations he ruled, without an interpreter.

notes.citation: Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus (ch. 18, Cineas's embassy to Rome)
notes.original: Plutarque en la vie de Pyrrh.
notes.gloss: Plutarch has Cineas at Rome; the feat of learning the names of the senators and knights the day after his arrival is told by Pliny (7.24.88) and Solinus.

notes.citation: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae, preface to book I (§ 2)
notes.original: Seneque au prologue de ſes declamations.
notes.gloss: Seneca says he could repeat two thousand names in the order given, and more than two hundred verses recited by his schoolfellows, from the last to the first; the same preface is cited at annot-021 {e}.

notes.original: Ciceron au j. des Tuſcula nes.
notes.gloss: Cicero's roll of memories: Simonides, Theodectes, Cineas, Charmadas, Metrodorus, Hortensius.

notes.citation: Solinus, at the place cited above (at {c})
notes.gloss: Au lieu deſſus allegué; the transcription's note breaks off at al-, and an is a wrong sort for au. Metrodorus of Scepsis is in Solinus's list; his being contemporary with Diogenes the Cynic is Coras's statement, not verified.

notes.citation: Pliny, Natural History, book 7, chapter 24 (7.24.88–90; the print's lieu vj read as liu. vij); Cicero, De oratore II (II.86–88, 351–360, the discourse on memory; II.74.299 on Themistocles) and Tusculan Disputations I (I.24.59)
notes.original: Pline au lieu vj c. xxiiij. ci ceron au ij. de Oratore & au j. des Tuſcula.
notes.gloss: Pliny names Cyrus, L. Scipio, Cineas, Mithridates, Charmadas, Metrodorus and Hortensius; Cicero's Greek is Charmadas, printed Charmides by Coras; Julius Caesar and Carneades are in neither list; Lucullus's memory is Cicero, Academica II.1–2. The same two authorities are cited together at annot-021 {a}.

notes.citation: Coras, Annotation XXI (cross-reference; the print's arno tation is a wrong sort for annotation)
notes.gloss: Annotation XXI compares du Tilh's memory to Scipio, Cyrus, Theodectes, Mithridates, Themistocles, Cineas, Metrodorus and Lucullus, with the protestation against comparing so impudent a man to such persons.

lines: accordé par ladite de Rols eſtre vray, &
depuis verifié, que les chauſſes y eſtoyẽt
Il ne me ſouuient point auoir leu qu'aucun homme
euſt la memoire ſi heureuſe, de ſe ſouuenir de tant d'a-
ctes particuliers des lieux, & des propos, de ſi long
temps, & à l'endroict de tant de perſonnes: hors mis
d'Adrian l'Empereur {a}. car Cyrus, Roy des Perſes, eſtãt
en ſon exercite grand, & nombreux, ſçauoit bien dire
tous le noms de ſes ſouldats, & genſdarmes: & faiſanr
la reueuë de ſon armee, parloit à chaſcũ par ſon nom {b}.
Ce que fit bien auſſi iadis à Rome Luce Scipion {c}.
Mithridates ſe ſouuenoit bien de vingtdeux langages:
d'autant de nations qu'il auoit ſoubz ſoy, parlãt à cha-
cune ſans interprete {d}. Cyneas ambaſſadeur de Pyrrhus,
dans vn iour qu'il fut à Rome, aprint bien tous les
noms des Senateurs & cheualiers Romains {e}, Seneque
ſçauoit bien comme luy meſme ſe vante, reciter deux
mille noms, par le meſme ordre qu'on les luy auoit
prononcez, & deux cens vers au rebours, commençant
au dernier {f}. Ce que deuant luy Theodectes, diſciple
au temps de Diogenes Cynique) faiſoit bien auſſi {h}.
On louë de meſme & beaucoup la memoire de Iule
Ceſar, Scipion, Luculle., Hortenſe, & de Porcius
Latro Romains: de Themiſtocles, Carneades & Char-
mides Grecs {i}. mais la memoire de ce du Thil ici, bien
qu'il euſt gaigné par aut, ou par vſage, ſurpaſſoit cõme
il ſemble: n'ayant eſté iamais deſcouuert par les cõmiſ-
ſaires, qu'il euſt failli d'vn ſeul iota. Ce que i'entens
auoir eſcrit, auec la proteſtation qu'ay ci deuant faite {k},
de ne vouloir entrer en comparaiſon d'vn ſi impudent
affrõteur auec perſonnes ſi nobles, grandes & illuſtres.
Or telles choſes ne peuuent tomber en
inſtruction qui luy fuſt donné par autre
